All right. Welcome,
and thank you for making the effort to come in today. I'll just introduce myself.
I'm Greg O'Connor. I'm the chair of the Select-- of the Petitions Committee.
Good day. Grant McPeamy, the deputy chair.
Nice to meet you.
Carl Weggs. I'm in for the Honorable Andrew Bayly,
sir.
Kia ora. Welcome. Selwyn Maib Brown. Cheers. Good evening.
Yes. All right. So now,
we've got you for 10 minutes. We've read your submissions, very
good submission.
And we'd love to hear from you, reiterate your
points, and hopefully leave time for questions.
Yes.
Thank you.
Kia ora koutou. Good afternoon. My name is Aida.
I'm a founding member of the Iranian Solidarity Group New Zealand.
Thank you for this opportunity to present to the committee on our petition.
This is
Arman, Arman Askarami. Arman is a member of the
Iranian Solidarity Group New Zealand.
He's also a lawyer who's worked for the community law
space, who's worked in the community law space, especially in
refugee and immigration law. And I'm now going to hand over to
Arman to present to the committee our oral submission.
Thank you.
Awesome.
Welcome, Arman.
Thank you very much for the opportunity.
So,
as you would've seen in the written submission, the petition is
about a family reunification pathway for Iranian
New Zealanders.
And we're seeking something modeled on the same precedent that the special
Ukraine visa was issued in 2022.
In terms of context, obviously there's been a war that's been ongoing
since February 28th, and
prior to that, a lot of protests and a lot of violence and
repression.
Estimates vary, but
suggest that upwards of 25,000 bombs have been dropped
between the US and Israel over the last few months.
We've also seen
a lot of civilian infrastructure that's been targeted, including
hospitals, water desalination plants, electrical
grids, schools, including a primary school in which
more than 100 children were killed on the very first day.
Airports, train stations,
residential areas,
and although in the last few days there's been a pause
in the bombing,
the situation is still very uncertain.
There's still a lot of uncertainty and instability in terms of
what comes next, and it's very fragile and very possible that
we might see full-scale war again, and there's been a lot of
back-and-forth threats. Threats of war crimes, things of this
nature.
In terms of the human toll, we know that thousands have already been
killed from the war so far. We know that thousands more have been
wounded. We know that millions have been displaced,
according to the Red Cross.
And of course, millions more have been traumatized because that's what war
does.
And so overall, there is really a bleak situation right
now, and there is a lot of hardship,
and a humanitarian crisis. And I'd point to
even MFAT has advised do not travel
for Iran. So, clearly there's an acknowledgment
of the difficult situation at the moment.
And so in this context, what we are
seeking is for support for the Iranian New Zealand
community, the same way that Ukrainian New Zealanders were
supported when the war started over there.
And so we're seeking a family reunification pathway modeled on the same
precedent.
Iranian New Zealanders are ready, willing, and able to fulfill any
sponsorship undertakings that are required.
And we think the total number that would be impacted here would
be small, at most in the low thousands.
We note that for the Ukraine visa, there were
2,293 temporary visas, and
ultimately only 480 people who got residency
through this pathway. So not a huge amount, but it would have
a really
meaningful impact on the community here.
And I can say, the community here, it's been a very difficult
situation and
a lot of Iranian New Zealanders have felt isolated and withdrawn and
depressed and I think this type of action can
help with social cohesion and
help people feel seen, heard, and valued.
I note that in some of the responses, there's been reference to
Immigration New Zealand providing further information
in terms of a phone line or how to apply for visas.
And while we appreciate that,
we submit that that doesn't ultimately assist the
situation because for any temporary visa
application, the applicant must be a bona fide
applicant, which is someone who genuinely intends a temporary
stay. And with the circumstances of war and
humanitarian crisis, it's a Really huge
hurdle to persuade Immigration New Zealand that anyone
really does
genuinely intend a temporary stay.
There was also reference to special direction requests as
well. I can speak from my time working in
community law. Those special direction requests are
very onerous. They're completely discretionary and
granted on an ad hoc basis.
So not really a sustainable solution for the
community here. And everybody has a family member
or family members
that we're deeply worried about.
Aside from the family reunification pathway, we'd also included in the
petition
something about an automatic visa extension for those currently in
the country on temporary visas, which MBA had said there was
1,017 Iranians on temporary visas as of May
And automatic visa extensions have been done, for example, during the COVID
pandemic. So it's something that's been done before.
But again, it's not huge numbers here, but it would really make a huge
difference for the community here.
And ultimately, we're just seeking the same compassion and empathy
that was afforded to Ukrainian New Zealanders during their time of
hardship.
All right. Thank you. Can I ask a question?
You've highlighted the fact this would be largely temporary and that
people would presumably go back to Iran
at the end of the war or at the end of the regime.
Because presumably, there are two overriding reasons here
why people want to leave Iran. Correct me if I'm
wrong, but there's the regime and then there's the war.
So we would have envisioned a pathway for residency if
people sought that. So
not necessarily just a temporary visa for ...
And that was the same with the special Ukraine visa.
There was an option to apply for residency that was introduced, which I said
450 Ukrainians did that.
I mean, both of those factors are
causing
hardship, but right now the war is the
main,
causing the most urgency and anxiety and
stress for our community.
If the regime remains in place and the war ends,
will those that come out under any visa such as this
be punished when they go back or likely to be disadvantaged when they go back
to Iran?
I probably couldn't speak in absolutes in terms
of how it would happen. I
would hesitate to say that anyone who migrates out, there would be
retribution or retaliation just for them leaving the country and coming back
in. Ultimately, what the Iranian government
does, I can't really speak for their mindset and
I'm sure there's a lot of things going through their minds in terms of what they
factor, so I can't really
speculate too much about that.
Thank you very much. Celia.
Thank you. Thank you for coming in, and thank you for also
sharing the Iranian culture, particularly through Nowruz and
so on.
Thank you for having me.
And
I was just interested in a couple of things.
I was looking at the comparison with the Ukrainian visa.
It
was open for two years. It's now closed, but sadly, the war
there continues. So how useful do you
think that has been for the Ukrainian ...
I mean, you may not know. That's fine.
Yeah. I mean, I'm sure there's areas for improvement
in terms of how that was rolled out, and that was certainly the first of its
kind to be done here. I think the point that we're
ultimately making is that there was the will there to try
and create a pathway for that community to be able to
sponsor their loved ones and just to
provide some type of assistance.
And so that's kind of the key point that we wanted to make.
Thank you. If I may, another couple of questions.
Sure.
Sadly, events at the moment
are impacting a number of countries in the same geographic
area.
The Greens have called, for example,
for
visas for Palestinian

us proceeding as a government with
the request from a number of different countries?

about consistency in terms of responding to various
humanitarian crises around the world.
I know that World Vision had recently launched an emergency
protection framework in terms of creating-
Okay
... a sort of humanitarian visa category.
I think Australia has something similar.
I think those are
worthy efforts and worth genuine consideration, and
yeah, I have complete sympathy for the Palestinians advocating for
something similar or any other community affected by war and hardship

Thank you.
All right.
Great.

Okay.

Can I respond to that? And thank you for-
Yeah. Yeah, sure

Yeah, sure

... of the Associate Minister's power, and they're not required to give reasons in

Yeah.
I've found, and some of my colleagues and former colleagues have found,
that
there's often a better chance when it's related to someone who's currently present
in the country,
whether their status has become unlawful or whether their visa pathway is
insecure.
Yeah.

world. And also a lot of Iranians are internally
displaced as well.
So they're not technically refugees because a refugee is someone outside of

It just makes things difficult. So I totally appreciate that point, but I don't

through special direction requests.
Yeah. No, I appreciate that. I totally understand, yeah, that obviously if there
was a special category that would be ideal.
But
just given-
Yeah

making in their response as well, is that there are, sadly,
with seemingly the world on fire, there are an
increasing number of places that are asking for the
same thing that you guys are asking for.
Which is why
I'm encouraged to hear that you're aware of that pathway and go for it.
It's just that within those ones there, there's just a lot of those.
Look, to me, based on my experience in the last couple of years, very compelling
cases to take to the Associate Immigration Minister.
Yeah.
All right. Look, well, thank you very much.
Don't ever underrate that you're obviously knocking on many
doors as you can.
And this is another way of making sure that
your, and that the stories
and particularly the situations of people you

Don't underestimate that even though there mightn't be an instant tick

are various, as my colleague
Greg has pointed out, there are various ways that these things can
be
assisted, helped if not resolved.
So thank you very much for making the effort to come in.
Yeah. Thank you very much.
Thank you.
Thank you.
You're
welcome.

A card addressed to the emergency department of a city hospital, which had the

It had the correct street name of the hospital, number, suburb, city, and

With no return address on the back, it would've been destroyed by New Zealand Post

it never got to the emergency department of the hospital, and the emergency
department would not know it was ever sent to them.
And this is New Zealand Post policy since May 2024.
In almost every case of an internet search for a postal
address of a main city hospital, the hospital's private bag
or post office number will not be displayed, only the physical street
address.
And so people address their mail to hospital patients as they find the address from
an internet search, and their cards are then to be returned to them.
And this is the policy of New Zealand Post since May 2024.
My brother-in-law here, John Boys, was a hospital chaplain for 25 years,
and he said how important it is in the recovery
process for hospital patients to receive cards and flowers.
Mm-hmm.
New Zealand Post policy since May 2024 is a
cost-saving measure, is to return to sender mail with the
correct postage and addressed in good faith to
existing physical street locations because New Zealand
Post's stated intention is not to extend its delivery
network by adding more street addresses to its database.
Posties around New Zealand continue to disobey New Zealand Post
instructions as they try to get mail delivered and not return to
sender.
Not only the Nelson Police Station and a hospital emergency department,
but we think tens of thousands of letters with clear addresses
and correct postage have been returned to the senders.
The volumes of returned mail have been steadily dropping, either
as more senders know it's important to use the box or private bag
number, or as they instead use the more expensive courier
bags. This is a very blunt, cold,
and uncaring behavior modification program
conducted by a state-owned enterprise answerable to this parliament.
There have been no news media statement of advice of the change in mail
addressing standards from New Zealand Post to the public.
The only news media alerts have come from the Postal Workers Union objecting
to this new policy.
I worked as a postie for 20 years, and like every other postie,
I used a markup book to ensure mail got to the intended recipient.
This was part of the service and factored into the price of a stamp.
However, New Zealand Post now wants to call this a free service and remove it as
cost saving. There is a definition in the Postal Services Act of mail
that could be returned to sender. Mail with a wrong or incomplete
address, or no such number, or illegible address, or
the address couldn't be found.
However, as a cost-cutting exercise, two years ago, New
Zealand Post invented a new classification out for
undeliverable postal items that are to be returned to sender,
and are now calling them non-valid postal address.
That is, mail that would no longer be redirected by the posties
from street addresses to the post office box or private bags where they existed.
There is no definition in the Postal Services Act of what New Zealand
Post calls non-valid postal address,
and any search of valid on the New Zealand Post website
only takes you to the postal codes finder.
So without reading through the full oral submission, there are some questions

Does the committee believe that the intention of Parliament
at the passage in-
Well, generally, John, it's up to us for the questions.
Okay. Is it? Oh, okay.
It can be-
Okay.

Okay. All right. What we'd like you to consider then perhaps.

We don't believe that the intention of Parliament at the passage of the

be returned to sender as a cost-saving exercise.
I'll put it as our considerations, if you like.
Um, well, we're not satisfied that Parliament intended when the act

article,
um, and then returning it to sender as a undeliverable

Um, we're not satisfied that New Zealand Post had the authority by

postal article and to establish a new process for dealing with these

Well, firstly, good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to attend this
hearing and to speak to the petition that this committee is currently considering.
My name is Matt Reardon. I'm the General Manager for Service Delivery at New
Zealand Post, where I'm responsible for the last mile delivery operation.
With me today is Matthew Kenning, our Government Relations Advisor.
We take it the committee has read our written submission, but I want to
quickly take the opportunity to make a couple of points before taking
questions. The issues raised in the petition relate
to operational changes we started two years ago in
2024, and I'm happy to discuss why we made these
changes. It's well understood that a physical address is not
always the same as a mail delivery address, and that many organizations have
separate postal addresses. The change we made two years ago
simply required mail to be sent to a valid delivery address
and stop the informal process of manually updating addresses when they were
wrong, which was time-consuming, costly, and not always accurate.
If mail items are addressed to a valid postal address and have the correct postage,
then our posties will deliver those mail items.
A valid postal address may include a location near or within a business
premise. We are open to businesses and other organizations asking to
register their physical addresses for delivery if they wish, if they meet our
criteria.
But we find that most don't want delivery to a physical address, such as an
unsecure roadside letterbox, and they prefer their PO box and
private bag.
Where
a mail item has a wrong address or isn't a valid postal address in our
network, we follow the usual return to sender processes.
We felt
like we ran a good process focusing on education for
senders and receivers when we made the change in 2024.
